en: The Essential Methods for the Five-Gate Dhyāna Sūtra,
composed by the Great Dhyāna Master Buddhamitra and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kaśmīra during the Song Dynasty.
The method of sitting meditation must have five gates:
first, ānāpāna; second, aśubha;
Third, the mind of loving-kindness;
fourth, contemplation of conditions;
fifth, mindfulness of the Buddha.
The three gates of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), impurity (*aśubha*), and contemplation of conditions (*pratyaya*) have both internal and external objects;
the two gates of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) take external objects as their conditions.
The reason there are five gates is that they accord with the illnesses of sentient beings:
if one has much mental distraction, one is taught *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing);
if one has much craving and attachment, one is taught *aśubha* (contemplation of impurity).
If one has much anger and hatred, teach them the mind of loving-kindness;
if one is deeply attached to the self, teach them dependent origination;
if the mind is sunken, teach them mindfulness of the Buddha.

If a practitioner has long possessed a virtuous mind but has not yet attained the Buddha-recollection samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), they should be instructed to contemplate the Buddha with a single-minded focus.

When contemplating the Buddha, one should, with utmost sincerity, visualize the Buddha’s physical marks and features until they are perfectly clear and distinct; once this is thoroughly understood, one should then close the eyes and maintain the recollection within the mind.
If the visualization is not clear, one should open the eyes again and look until the mind is fully lucid, and only then return to sitting.
With body upright and mind composed, he focused his mindfulness before him as if facing the true Buddha, perceiving it with perfect clarity and no difference.
He then rose from his seat, knelt, and addressed the teacher, saying:
"In my room, I have perceived the Buddha through focused mindfulness, no different from this."
The Master said, "Return to your original seat, fix your mindfulness upon your forehead, and recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion.
At that moment, images of the Buddha appeared upon his forehead, starting from one up to ten, and finally becoming immeasurable.

If the practitioner sees many Buddhas emerging from the forehead, or if they return after traveling not far from the body, the teacher should know that this person is one who seeks the state of a śrāvaka.
If [the Buddha] returns after a short distance, he is one seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
If he returns from a great distance, he is a follower of the Mahāyāna.

When the Buddhas emerging from these three types return close to his body, they turn the earth into gold; all these Buddhas then enter the earth, which becomes as level as the palm of a hand and as clear and bright as a mirror.
One observes one’s own body as bright and pure as the earth; this is called attaining the sphere of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
Having attained this sphere, one informs the teacher.
The teacher says:
"This is a sublime state.
This is called the contemplation of the first gate.
The Master further instructed him to fix his mindfulness upon the heart and then contemplate the Buddha.

One immediately sees all the Buddhas emerge from the heart, each holding a lapis lazuli staff; from both ends of the staff emerge those of the Three Vehicles, with the flames of light varying in size.
Having thus emerged, the last Buddha stands upright with the staff held at his heart. This final Buddha then turns his body and re-enters, followed by all the Buddhas who had previously gone out.
If a follower of the Hīnayāna enters this state of exhaustion, they remain there;

if a follower of the Mahāyāna enters this state of exhaustion, light issues forth from every pore of their body, filling the four seas, extending upward to the Peak of Existence and downward to the limits of the wind. Having thus illuminated all, it returns and re-enters the body, which becomes like pure lapis lazuli.
The reason the radiance returns and enters his body is to manifest the marks and signs of a realm that is courageous, powerful, and swift.
Having done so, he immediately went to inform his teacher.
The teacher said:
"This is called the application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna); it is named 'application of mindfulness' because it can give rise to all meditative concentrations.
It is also the first attainment of this Dharma.
All of these are what the disciples of the Buddhas have attained; they are not what is seen by the seers of heterodox paths or immortals."
The upper staff is the mark of meditative concentration.
The light of the marks is the mark of wisdom.
This is the mark of the stage of the ordinary person within [the path].
The teacher further instructed him, saying:
"From now on, abandon the two previous meditations and fix your mind upon your navel.
He then followed the teacher's instruction and single-mindedly contemplated his navel.
After observing the disk for a short while, he perceived that it had signs of movement;
yet, gazing intently without distraction, he saw a substance within the disk, resembling a wild goose egg in its brilliant white color.
He immediately went to inform his teacher.
The teacher said,
"Go and look again at the place where it is."

Following the teacher's instruction, he visualized that within his own body there was a lotus flower with a stem of lapis lazuli and a pericarp of gold; upon the pericarp sat a Buddha in the full lotus posture.
From the navel of the first Buddha, another lotus flower emerges, upon which a Buddha again sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

In this manner, they emerge one after another until reaching the great ocean. At the edge of the ocean, the final first Buddha returns into the navel of the second Buddha; the second Buddha returns into the navel of the third Buddha; and so on, returning successively until reaching the Buddha at the human navel.

Once each Buddha has been made to enter the center of the practitioner's body, lotus flowers emerge from every pore of the practitioner’s own body, filling the void of space like hanging jeweled necklaces.
When they are thus born, they see all the lotuses enter their navels.

At that time, the practitioner’s body becomes supple, light, and joyful; they see their own body as bright and pure, with a color like various precious gems. They then report what they have seen to the master.
The Master said:
"Excellent. You must apply your mind well and contemplate this body until the signs of meditative concentration are achieved."
The master instructed him, saying,
"Observe the interior once more.
He then observed as directed and saw five-colored flames of light upon his crown.
Having seen this, he informed his teacher.
The teacher said, "Observe further; the five lights possess five auspicious signs."

Having observed thus according to the instructions, he saw a Buddha sitting cross-legged within the radiance; he further examined what auspicious signs were present among the Buddhas within the five rays of light.
He immediately saw various lotus flowers emerge from the Buddha’s mouth; having emerged, they filled the entire earth.

He was further instructed to observe one of the Buddhas within the five lights, and he saw five lions emerge from that Buddha’s navel. Once the lions had emerged, they consumed all the flowers that had been produced, and then returned into the navel of the Buddha within the five lights.
Once the lion has entered, the five lights and the Buddha likewise enter through the crown of his head.
This is called the meditative sign of the Lion’s Display Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*).
Furthermore, as the practitioner observes the light entering the Buddha’s body, their own body becomes golden in color.
Having seen the golden color, he saw something within the navel-circle, round like the sun or moon, white and bright and pure.
Having seen it, he informed his teacher.
The teacher said:
“Observe further.
He immediately saw Buddhas emerging from his armpits until they filled them, and Buddhas emerging from within his waist; in all, four Buddhas emerged.

Once the four Buddhas had emerged, he saw the bodies of these four Buddhas, and from each individual Buddha there emerged immeasurable orbs of sunlight, the radiance of which was exceedingly bright and pure.

By means of the rays of the sun, one perceives the forms of the four continents; from the Peak of Existence above down to the limit of the wind below, all are clearly discerned, without any obstruction, as if looking into the palm of one's hand.
This is called the realm of the pure white liberation.
Having seen this, he again sees the four Buddhas emerging from their respective places and returning back into them.

Once the four Buddhas have entered, he further sees various white flames and rays of light entering from the front and exiting from the back, exiting from the back and entering from the front, entering from the left and exiting from the right, and entering from the right and exiting from the left.
When these four types of inhalation and exhalation have been completed, one sees one’s own body as luminous and pure, as well as a perfect, pure radiance surrounding the water on all four sides.
This is called the stage of luminous purity.
Having seen this light, one attains what is called the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) while within the fourth dhyāna.

For a practitioner of the gate of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), when a virtuous mind arises and they approach their teacher, before receiving the teaching, the teacher first instructs them to sit upright in the meditation hall for seven days.

If there is one who possesses the requisite conditions, they will perceive a throbbing sensation in their body and at the navel; they will clearly see their own body, and upon the nail of the big toe of the left foot, there will be white dew like a pearl.
The practitioner rises from his seat and reports what he has perceived to the teacher.
The teacher instructs the practitioner on the postures of walking, standing, sitting, and standing still.
If that person’s internal objects of perception are numerous, and their gaze is fixed upon things extremely high and far away, one knows that external conditions are predominant.
If one walks slowly with a single-minded focus, observing and examining with discernment, one knows that the object of perception is internal.
If the object is external, he is instructed to contemplate corpses in a charnel ground.
Having seen them, he returns to his room and sits, contemplating his own body.

If one can maintain the visualization of the bones for three days without losing it, one next contemplates all the people within the room, gradually causing them to appear as white bones, continuing this sequence until it reaches the great ocean.
By what signs does one reach the great ocean?
It is by perceiving the source of the waves in the water.

All the skeletons and one’s own body are adorned with jeweled necklaces; furthermore, one sees a great flood of water come and pour over the crown of the head, filling the entire body. Once the body is filled, it causes blood to flow from the toes, forming a river of blood.
This is called the samādhi of revulsion.
Again, focusing his mindfulness on what was before, he saw that everything had lain down and only his own body remained.
He reported this to his teacher.
The Master said:
"Observe for yourself and divide it into five parts.
The reason for dividing it into five parts is that one wishes to know internal awareness and external awareness as a means of verification.

If one can analyze the body into its five constituent parts, one will know that there is no self in it now, nor is there a self in each individual part; thus, the mind abides in the gateway of the concentration on non-self.

If, while dwelling in meditative concentration, one sees blades emerge from every joint and limb, with bright flames issuing from each blade's edge, this is called the sphere of the wisdom of selflessness.
Furthermore, fix the mind once more upon the white bones; one will see a bright star emerge from atop the bones, with golden spheres surrounding it on all four sides.
The "star" refers to the luminous and pure realm.
The "Golden Ball" refers to the twenty-fifth stage, the realm of wisdom.
This is called the fulfillment of the realm of white bones.
It is a concise extraction of the sign of white bones from among the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*).

Although the practitioner sees white bones, they may still give rise to thoughts of attachment toward the physical forms of men and women; to eliminate this attachment, one should contemplate the thirty-six impure substances.

When contemplating, one should fix the mind upon the forehead. After fixing the mind for a short while, a bright pearl will appear before one on the forehead; one must not let it fall, so that the mind may remain firmly established.
The reason these signs appear is that they flow forth from the present life.

Before long, he instructs him to release [the light] so that it enters the earth; having entered the earth, he follows it with his observation as it descends clearly and purely, passing beyond the earth element.
The reason for this knowledge is that one sees one’s own body and, in various places, sees ice and frost exceeding the element of wind.
The reason for this knowledge is that the softness of the body exceeds the element of water.
The reason for this knowledge is that one sees one's own body and water everywhere, with bubbles emerging upon it as it reaches the wind element.
The reason for this knowledge is that one sees one's own body as being like a *gaganagañja* (sky-treasure) jewel.
If one seeks the void and returns, bright, pure radiance follows the jewel and comes forth.
Once the jewel has emerged and entered the practitioner’s navel, having entered, one perceives the thirty-six components clearly and without obstruction.
At that time, the practitioner attains the completion of the fixed perception of the male or female form.
Regarding the method of the white bone contemplation (*śvetāsthi-bhāvanā*):
having completely removed the flesh, blood, sinews, and veins of the body, the bones remain supporting one another, white as jade or snow, and their radiance is likewise so.
If one does not see [it], it is like a leper to whom a physician says to his family:
"If you can have him drink blood that is the same color as milk, he may then be cured."
He had everything in the house made known, and had silver vessels fashioned to hold blood, saying:
"Drink this milk; this illness will surely be cured.
The patient said:
"It is blood," he replied.
"A white substance will cure it."
"Do you not see that all the objects in your home are entirely white? It is because of your transgressions that you see them as blood.
You should simply concentrate your mind on the appearance of milk; do not think of it as blood."
In this manner, after seven days, it transformed into milk; how much more so for one who cannot see the actual white [substance]?
He then beheld a skeleton, and within that skeleton, he saw the arising and ceasing of the mind continuing in succession like beads strung on a thread.
The same applies to what is seen and to the contemplation of the external body.
If the mind dwells thus with diligence and does not abandon it, it is like seeing smoke when drilling for fire, or seeing mud when digging a well—one will obtain water before long.
If the mind abides in stillness and, with eyes open, one perceives the bones as clearly as if water were limpid, then one will see the reflected image;
if it is turbid, one does not see it.

In the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, the Buddha is the Dharma King who can enable people to attain various wholesome dharmas; therefore, those who practice seated meditation should first bring the Buddha to mind.

The Buddha can cause immeasurable sins to become thin and slight, enabling one to attain various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). When one recollects the Buddha with a sincere mind, the Buddha likewise recollects that person.
Being recollected by the King [of Dharma], enemies and creditors cannot approach or harm them;
it is the same when recollecting the Buddha—other evil dharmas cannot disturb or confuse them.
If one practices mindfulness of the Buddha, how can one recollect him when the Buddha is not present in the world?
A person’s self-confidence is nothing greater than that of their own eyes; therefore, one should contemplate the image as if seeing the true Buddha, no different from the reality.
First, one should contemplate each mark clearly, proceeding from the uṣṇīṣa and the white tuft between the eyebrows down to the feet, and then back up to the uṣṇīṣa.
Returning to a quiet place, close the eyes and reflect, fixing the mind upon the image so that no other thoughts arise; if any other conditions should occur, restrain them and bring the mind back.
When one observes with the mind and perceives as desired, this is called attaining the concentration of contemplation on conditions (*ālambana-samādhi*).
One should form this thought:
"Neither do I go there, nor does the image come here; that I am able to see it is due to the mind’s stable dwelling upon its conceptualization."
Once one has attained the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, one may subsequently advance to contemplate the physical body (janmakāya), seeing it as if face-to-face with no difference.
Since the human mind is prone to wandering and frequently conditions itself toward unwholesome dharmas, one should guard it just as a nurse watches over her child, preventing them from doing evil.
If the mind does not abide [in concentration], one should reproach oneself:
"The sufferings of old age, illness, and death constantly come to press upon me.
Yet, if I am born in the heavens and become attached to exquisite desires, there will be no wholesome dharmas to discipline the mind."
"If I fall into the three evil realms, I will suffer from affliction and terror, and a virtuous mind will not arise.
Therefore, within this very body, I must now recollect the Buddha with a sincere heart.
He further thought to himself:

"To be born in the final age when the Dharma is about to perish is like beating a drum to release prisoners from an open gate: as the sound of the drum gradually fades and the gate closes one leaf, how can one not realize for oneself that one must seek to escape from prison?"
Since beginningless time in the past, throughout the cycle of birth and death, we have undergone myriad forms of suffering and affliction.

Now that we have merely begun to receive the Dharma, we have not yet attained its fulfillment; the thief of impermanent death constantly comes to assail us, and we endure the sufferings of birth and death for incalculable eons.

In this way, through various forms of self-reproach, one causes the mind to abide in the sign; while sitting, lying down, or walking, one constantly beholds the Buddha. Thereafter, one further advances to the visualization of the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
Once meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) has been attained, it becomes progressively easier to cultivate the visualization of the physical body.

Regarding the contemplation of the Dharma-body: since the mind has already achieved success through following its perceptions while contemplating the image, one will immediately behold it upon withdrawing the mind and entering meditative concentration.
One should rely on the image to bring about mindfulness of the birth-body.
He observed that [the Buddha] appeared as if sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, his radiance manifest and his features most extraordinary;
he was also like when, in the Deer Park, he preached the Dharma of the Four Truths to the five bhikṣus.

Furthermore, when the Great Radiance was emitted from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and the Prajñāpāramitā was preached for the great assembly, if one applies oneself to any single point, fixing mindfulness before one so that it does not scatter outward, and if the mental image becomes stable, one will immediately see the Buddha; the entire body will experience such bliss that it penetrates to the very marrow of the bones.
For example, it is like finding a cool pond in the heat or a warm chamber in the cold; no worldly pleasure can serve as a metaphor for this.

One who contemplates the Dharma-body has already seen the Buddha’s birth-body within emptiness; one should now, by means of the contemplation of the birth-body, perceive the internal Dharma-body—the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and immeasurable wholesome karmas.
It is like a person who first sees a golden vase and subsequently observes the mani-jewel within it.

Therefore, the Dharmakāya is truly wondrous and its divine wisdom is incomparable; there is neither near nor far, neither difficulty nor ease. All immeasurable worlds are as if before one's eyes, such that there is not a single dharma that is not known, and all dharmas are fully understood.
Therefore, the practitioner should always maintain focused mindfulness so as not to allow the mind to scatter; if it attends to other objects, one should collect it and bring it back.
Furthermore, all those whose lives have ended know that at the time of death, they first lose their sense faculties.
It is like being cast into a pit of fire, where one’s cry reaches as far as the Brahma Heaven.

There is nothing more terrifying than the thief of death; only the Buddha alone possesses the power to rescue and deliver, bestowing upon all beings of the human and celestial realms the bliss of nirvana.
Furthermore, all Buddhas, throughout their successive lives, have never begrudged their own bodies or lives for the sake of all sentient beings.
For example, when Śākyamuni Buddha was a prince and went out on an excursion, he saw a man suffering from leprosy and immediately commanded his physician, saying:
"One must drink the blood of an immortal and smear his marrow upon him; only then can he be cured."
The Prince thought to himself:
"Such a person is difficult to find.
Even if one were found, he could not be harmed; for with each error comes death."
He then gave his own body to him to treat.

The Buddha is likewise for all sentient beings; the Buddha’s kindness is profound and heavy, exceeding even that of one's parents. Even if all sentient beings were to constitute one part, while the second part should be devoted to mindfulness of the Buddha, one should not harbor other thoughts.
By practicing in accordance with these various merits through mindfulness,
if this mindfulness is perfected, one will sever the fetters and even attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
If various illnesses should arise during this interval, one should take medicine according to the specific ailment.

If one does not attain meditative concentration, one will become the most noble and honored among the six heavens of the desire realm; by the power of one's karmic conduct, a palace will follow one of its own accord, or one will be born before the various Buddhas—there is no uncertainty in this.
It is like a person who mixes medicinal herbs with red copper; if it does not become gold, it will at least not lose its silver nature.

When one contemplates the Buddhas of the ten directions and recollects the Buddhas of the ten directions, sitting and gazing toward the east, there appears a vast and expansive light. All mountains, rivers, and rocky cliffs vanish, and one sees only a single Buddha seated in the full lotus posture, raising his hand to preach the Dharma.

With clear mental observation, the marks and signs of radiance become vividly manifest; fix the mind upon the Buddha without allowing other objects to arise, and if the mind wanders to other thoughts, withdraw it and bring it back.
One who perceives in this manner increases the number of Buddhas by ten;
having seen them, they further increase to a hundred, a thousand, and even to infinite bodies.
As for those nearby, they cause them to become increasingly distant and increasingly vast, until one sees only the various Buddhas with their lights interconnecting.
When one has attained such [realization] through mental clarity and observation, one turns the mind toward the southeast and contemplates as before.
Once this is accomplished, one does the same for the northwest, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

Having already seen all the Buddhas in every direction, one should further, at once, contemplate all the Buddhas of the ten directions, perceiving them all simultaneously within a single moment of mental focus.

One who has accomplished a concentrated mind sees all the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma within that concentration; the net of doubt is entirely removed, and they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

If, due to the conditions of past offenses, one does not see the Buddhas, one should repent, entreat [the Buddhas], and rejoice in merit during the six periods of the day and night for a single day and night; gradually, one will naturally come to see them.
Even if they do not preach the Dharma in response to one's entreaties, that person’s mind will remain joyful and their body peaceful and free from affliction.

When first practicing the method of seated meditation, one is first taught to focus the attention on the big toe of the right foot and observe it becoming swollen; then, using the mind to scratch at it, one causes yellow fluid to flow out like pus and blood until the flesh is completely rotted away and only white bones remain.
If they see [the bones] completely, one should extensively teach them the meditation on the skeleton (*asthi-bhāvanā*).
If they see it filling the entire world-system, one should teach them the Mahāyāna.
If they see it nearby, one should teach them the Hīnayāna.

Instruct them to focus their attention on the tip of the nose and contemplate that the flesh and muscles of the human body are all formed from the impure vital essence of one's parents; next, they should observe the white teeth, reflecting that within the human body there is nothing but these white bones.
If one sees long teeth or white hair on the forehead, one should immediately contemplate the bones until the entire body becomes white, extending far and near as described above.

Depending on the depth or shallowness of this person's roots of merit, if they cannot suddenly see the white bones when instructed, one should teach them the usual nine-fold contemplation (*navasamjñā*) and have them practice for one month or one autumn; they must see the white bones before proceeding.

If you see sentient beings being taught to contemplate the mind of loving-kindness or the contemplation of dharmas, or being taught to maturely contemplate white bones, and you see them contemplating other things, you should say to those people:
"This is also good; however, set this matter aside for now and simply contemplate white bones."
If, while previously observing the white bones for a long time,
one perceives warmth within one's own body,
instruct them to continue the observation.
When one perceives warmth and feels secure, peaceful, and joyful, this is the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*).
Next, one should instruct them to mentally resolve upon the white bones, causing each joint to dissolve.
If you see other objects, you should set them aside for the time being and focus solely on the disintegration of the white bones.
After observing this for a long duration, if you say:
"Fire issues forth from the crown of my head."
He was instructed to observe further,
saying:
"I always see fire issuing from the crown of my head."
Within the body there is peace and bliss, and no distracted thoughts; this is the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

Next, instructing him to focus his attention until the bones become white and pure, they then scatter and fall to the ground like snow upon the earth, or like crumbled soil, with various strange objects such as white light appearing upon them.
He was instructed to observe it further.
If he says:
"I continue to see such pleasure within my body."
One should say to them:
"Try to recall and think of a person you loved in the past, and perform worldly affairs with them.
Having reflected upon this, they will say:
"When I recall people, I see them only as transformations of pus, blood, and impurities, which are most loathsome to behold.
Next, he taught him to contemplate the body as being like a bundle of grass or like an empty leather bag.
If they say,
"I see my own body as like a bundle of dry grass or an empty leather bag; when it is completely consumed by fire,
then there is no 'self' at all," instruct them to observe further:
"Observe from where your thought arises when it arises,
and from where it ceases when it ceases. Regarding this observation,
the essential instruction is as follows:
"I observed that when a thought suddenly arises, it originates from the mind; when it ceases, it ceases at the tip of the nose.
When it ceases at the tip of the nose, the body becomes tranquil and still within, and one no longer perceives a self—this is clear and distinct."
He instructed him to observe the crown of his head, saying:

"I see my body grow large; water issues from the crown of my head and fills the interior of my body until it is completely full, then it emerges evenly from the midpoint and flows onto the ground before me."
Once the water had completely flowed out, he instructed him to submerge himself again, making his body appear coarse and large.
[The disciple] said:
"I see my body has become large; the water fills its interior, and when it flows out, it forms a great pool."
He instructs him to pour ghee as an empowerment so that it enters his body.
If he says, "I have been empowered with ghee; my body has become vast," [the master should respond accordingly].
He instructed him to observe it closely. He said:

"Observe for a brief moment until you see smoke arise from the skin; then the fire will blaze up and fill the body. Extinguish it with water so that the fire is quenched and you may quickly regain your composure."
He instructed him to observe the pond with focused attention.
He replied:
"I see that there is naturally a tree in the pond, and the tree bears sweet fruit."
Having seen this fruit, if there are sentient beings who come seeking food due to hunger, those who observe them should immediately give rise to loving-kindness and contemplate their own bodies.
If one says:

"I observe my own body as entirely flowing with pus and blood onto the ground; when sentient beings see it, they take it and eat it, and once they have eaten their fill, they each depart in the four directions."
He was instructed to observe his own body and the bodies of others.
He then said:
"I see many hungry ghosts coming to my side, oppressed by hunger, their lives as fragile as a single hair."
He then instructs them to give their bodies with a mind of loving-kindness.
If they say,
"I give my body so that [beings] may be fully satisfied," [he approves].
He was instructed to observe further.
He then said:
"I see countless sentient beings surrounding me on all four sides."
If one sees this, one should be taught to observe one's own body.
If one says:
"I see my own body as impure, full of pus and blood, lying upon the ground; when sentient beings see it, they take it up and eat it."
Once they were fully satiated, he instructed them to observe closely:
"I see that suddenly a fire has broken out, burning the various sinners as well as my own body; everything that was within the waters of the pond has now completely vanished."
Furthermore, he was instructed to observe closely the locus of perception. He said:
"I see the sentient beings and the water in the pond, and my own body has all returned to its former state."
He observes other sentient beings as well as his own body.
He thinks:
"I see my own milk flowing out and falling upon the ground, yet these sentient beings cannot obtain it to eat because their transgressions are so heavy."
He was instructed to practice the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). He said:

"In a mere moment, my milk turns into pus; when sentient beings are in desperate hunger, they devour it. Once they are satiated, I see fire blazing from the soles of their feet, burning all sentient beings until they suddenly perish."
Once the practitioner has seen this matter, they should be instructed to make a vow not to undergo rebirth again.
They should then be taught to immediately observe the aforementioned pond. If they say:
"I beheld a pond, within which the branches and leaves of lotus trees were lush and flourishing.

Having seen this, I entered the water and sat beside the cluster of trees; I then observed fire issuing from my own body and filling the pond. In an instant, a fire suddenly broke out, burning my own body as well as that of sentient beings, until the water in the pond was completely exhausted."
Following these instructions, he observed further. He said:
"I see that trees have suddenly grown in the pond; their branches and leaves are lush and flourishing, and they produce sweet fruit."
When the practitioner sees this, they approach the tree to eat the fruit.
Once they have eaten their fill, their body and mind become clear, pure, peaceful, and blissful.
Thus, one is taught to practice pure observation of this pond and of one's own body.
If one says,
"In a mere instant, it has all completely withered away," and the practitioner,
seeing this sign of destruction, feels fear and dread in his heart, he immediately comes to inform the teacher.
The teacher should instruct him in the contemplation of the body as the root of suffering, causing him to contemplate the body so that it becomes like foam or bubbles.
If he says:
"I see my own body as being like foam or bubbles," and [he sees] bones emerge from the body, and having emerged, he uses his hand to rub them flat like flour to form the ground.
He then further instructed him to contemplate the body as being like a bellows.

If he says, "I am contemplating myself as being like a bellows," then immediately the bones emerge; these bones are so subtle that when rubbed, they smear upon the ground, and that ground becomes blue in color.
He further instructs them to contemplate the body:
"If one says:
'I contemplate my own body as minute particles, and from the body emerge bones; those bones are pitch black, which, when ground, become earth.'"
He instructed him to observe his own body and to observe the earth.
He replied:
"I observed that a snake emerged from the pond; its body was red like fire. As the snake approached my body, it transformed into fire and began to burn my body."
Thus it happened seven times.
Then, water spontaneously appeared within the assembly and sprinkled upon him, whereupon his snake body immediately vanished.
[The Buddha] further instructed him to again contemplate his own body and to contemplate the earth.
If one says:
"I observe that in a mere moment a natural light emerges, lofty, brilliant,
and beautiful," and immediately thereafter observes the body again.
If one says:

"I perceive a sense of harmony and well-being; my mind is joyful and free from weariness, and a natural radiance comes forth, pervading and filling my entire body," then instruct them to observe their own bodies in this manner seven times.
If one says:
"I myself saw light upon my crown, resembling a cloud-canopy, its color like silver," and this matter is fully established, it should be understood as the first path;
it is also called the completion of the contemplation of fire.
Next, observe the water element; instruct them to observe which parts of the body contain water.
If they say, "The entire body is water," [proceed as follows].
He should instruct him to observe further.
If he says,
"I see water appearing within my eye," that is good.
If he does not become attached, [the teacher] asks:
"Observe where the water above your head comes from? If he says:
"I see water emerging from my eyes, yet it does not fall to the ground.
The eyes are like foam, and the head is likewise filled with it.
The teacher should then ask:
"What do you see when you look at the water?
What characteristics does it have when it emerges?
He replied:
"I see that within my head it is neither warm nor cold. "Excellent!
If you say the water is warm, know that it is not the true state; I shall further instruct you to observe again, so that the water being neither warm nor cold becomes the true reality."
Instruct them to visualize from the throat and chest downward into the abdomen as being filled with water, but do not allow it to enter the arms and legs.
The water must be the color of crystal.
If one perceives the water as warm, then it is real; otherwise, it is not real.
Next, observe the body through to the arms and feet.
If one says:
"I see that this is merely the appearance of a leather bag."
Furthermore, one sees houses, beds, and seats filled with water.
That which is cold water is the real; the rest is not real.
It is most excellent if one sees the water extensively.
Next, one contemplates from where the water element is exhausted.
If one says:
"I see the water within my own body being consumed until it is gone; there remains only empty skin, like a bundle of straw, which is then completely burned away by fire, leaving no self at all."
The contemplation of the water element is concluded.
Next, one contemplates the fire element, instructing them to observe the four sides and ask: "Where is there fire?
If they say:

If someone says, "I see fire arising from the crown of my head," or says it emerges from the nose, or says it emerges from the mouth, or says it emerges from the eyes or ears, instruct them to observe further.
He replied, "I see five-colored lights emerging from my nose, their appearance like threads, and my body is neither warm nor cold.
This is one method; he was instructed to observe it further.
If they say,
"I see fire emerging from the crown of my head," or "It emerges from the lower orifice," instruct them to observe further.
He said:
"I see fire upon my head like the form of a cloud-canopy, or sometimes below me like the form of a cloud; my body is serene, joyful, and at peace.
This is one method; he was instructed to further contemplate the body.
He said, "I see fire emerging from my navel, resembling a lotus flower in color like gold.
This was excellent; he was instructed to contemplate the fire within his body.
If one says:
"I constantly see fire while walking and sitting; it is not only when I am sitting.
When I walk, I see the fire as if someone were carrying a torch and walking, always appearing with great brilliance before me."
"Then others may indeed find it strange, yet others truly do not see it, while the body remains constantly warm.
This is one method; teach them to observe it further for a long time.
He said:
"I see within the waters of the great ocean a maṇi jewel, from which flames issue forth like fire.
This jewel is, in fact, a single dharma.
The contemplation of the fire element is concluded.
Next is the contemplation of the wind element; because its nature is subtle and minute, it is not explained here as it is beyond the scope of detailed analysis.
These four great elements are the fundamental basis for seated meditation; although many other signs may be seen, one must ultimately direct oneself toward these four contemplations.

In the initial instruction for contemplating the Buddha, one first teaches the practice of sitting in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), ensuring that the mind does not wander toward external conditions or objects.
Thereafter, one leads the practitioner before a physical image, instructing them to contemplate the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) with clear discernment.
Then, sitting comfortably, instruct them to use their mind’s eye to contemplate the marks and signs of this image.
If they say,
"I see the image clearly," [proceed accordingly].
This is one matter.
He instructs them to observe their own bodies, causing the body to sit peacefully, and instructs them to return to observing the Buddha.
If he says:
"I see one Buddha up to ten Buddhas, making them all clearly manifest"—
these are the two matters.
He instructs [the practitioner] to carefully observe his own body until it gradually becomes peaceful, and then instructs him to return to observing the Buddhas.
If one says:
"I clearly see ten Buddhas up to twenty Buddhas," these are the three matters.
Instruct them to observe their own bodies so that the bodies become increasingly peaceful and pure, and then instruct them to return to observing the Buddha.
If they say:
"I see twenty Buddhas up to fifty Buddhas, as clearly as before," [then proceed accordingly].
These are the four matters.
He teaches one to contemplate one's own body so that the mind becomes increasingly subtle, and he teaches one to turn back and contemplate the Buddha.
If it is said:
"I see fifty Buddhas up to a hundred Buddhas, their marks and signs being as described before.
These are the five matters.
[The teacher] instructs [the student] to observe his own body so that the mind becomes increasingly subtle, and then instructs him to return to observing the Buddha.
If one says:
"I have seen from one hundred Buddhas up to one thousand Buddhas,
clearly as before," these are the six matters.
He is taught to observe his own body so as to cause the mind to become increasingly subtle, and is further taught to observe the Buddha.
If he says:
"I see two hundred Buddhas up to four hundred Buddhas, which is clearer and more excellent than before."
These are the seven matters.
He instructs [the practitioner] to observe his own body so as to cause the mind to become increasingly subtle, and instructs him to turn back and observe the Buddha.
If he says:
"I see four hundred Buddhas up to eight hundred Buddhas, whose marks and signs become increasingly radiant.
These are the eight matters.
[The teaching] instructs one to observe one's own body so as to make the mind increasingly subtle, and then further instructs one to observe the Buddha.
If one says,
"I have seen eight hundred Buddhas up to a thousand Buddhas," these are the nine matters.

From one Buddha to a thousand Buddhas, he contemplates their physical marks and signs until they are extremely clear; then, turning back to observe his own body as impure pus and blood, he immediately teaches the practice of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
If you see white bones, immediately practice the contemplation of white bones (*asthi-saṃjñā*).
If you see sentient beings suffering in pain, immediately practice the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*).
If you do not see these things, return to contemplating a single Buddha, with a sincere and earnest heart, seeking compassion and repenting.
This is the beginner practitioner’s contemplation of the Buddha-dharma.
If one is approaching the stage of abiding, one should contemplate the Buddha extensively.
If one says:
"I see one Buddha up to hundreds of thousands of millions, even to a vast multitude of Buddhas, their marks and signs clearly manifest.
This is the tenth matter.
It teaches one to contemplate one's own body so that it becomes bright and pure, and then to turn back and contemplate the Buddha, giving rise to great vows and a mind of offering.
He said:
"I have seen immeasurable Buddhas; before each Buddha there were flowers that appeared spontaneously, which I took and offered until they completely filled [the space].
This is the eleventh matter.
He instructs them to observe their own bodies so as to make them clear and pure, and then further instructs them to observe the Buddha.
If they say,
"As I have already seen [the Buddha] before, my heart gives rise to joy," [he instructs them to proceed].
He was instructed to contemplate the Buddha with a sincere mind, desiring to make offerings. He said:

"I see a tree of flowers spontaneously emerge; upon it grow various flowers of many colors. Spontaneously, a person appears who takes these exquisite flowers and gives them to me. I offer them by scattering them over all the Buddhas, causing them to be distributed everywhere so that the flowers are never exhausted."
These are the twelve matters.

Next, he instructs him to sit before the Buddha and contemplate his own body until it is extremely bright and pure. He further instructs him to begin the contemplation from the east, directing the mind eastward to see countless Buddhas, ceasing only when the mind becomes weary.
These are the thirteen matters.
Having instructed him regarding the preceding boundary, he proceeds next to the east.
If he says:
"I intended to travel eastward and saw countless Buddhas filling the void without limit or boundary; only when my mind grew weary did I cease.
Yet, as I again turned my mind to travel eastward, it stopped only when it encountered a limit or obstruction. It was the same in the south, west, and north."
These are the fourteen matters.
He instructs [the practitioner] to observe the limbs and joints within his own body until they are all clearly understood.
If he says:
"If you see me," he taught,
"return and look at the soles of my feet.
If one says:
“I see various lights beneath the Buddha’s feet, which then spread back out to the four directions, where all Buddhas are present within lotuses atop those lights.
These are the fifteen matters.
Instruct them to give rise to a mind of joy by contemplating the Buddha, observing his feet closely.
If they say,
"I see light emanating from the soles of the Buddha's feet, reaching the great earth without limit," [then proceed accordingly].
He instructs them to contemplate by means of this light.
If they say:
"I see immeasurable and boundless sentient beings suffering in pain; wherever the light shines, all are completely at peace."
These are the sixteen matters.
He instructs him to contemplate his own body so that it becomes further transformed into clarity and purity, and instructs him to contemplate the center of a single Buddha.
If he says:
“I saw light emanate from between the Buddha’s eyebrows, pervading to the furthest reaches of the four directions, where all Buddhas abide upon that light.
This is the seventeenth matter.
Instruct them to seek the vision by following the light. If they say:
"I see immeasurable people appearing within the light, all experiencing happiness," [then proceed accordingly].
These are the eighteen matters.
He instructs [the practitioner] to contemplate his own body until it becomes extremely clear and pure, and then instructs him to turn back and contemplate the two breasts of a single Buddha.
If he says:
"I saw light spontaneously emerge from between the Buddha's two breasts, pervading the four directions, with all Buddhas situated upon that light.
This is the nineteenth matter.
Instruct them to seek and contemplate the light.
If they say,
"I see within this light immeasurable people, all experiencing happiness," [instruct them as follows].
These are the twenty matters.
He is taught to observe his own body and see the body with extreme clarity, and is taught to turn back and observe the space between the eyebrows of a single Buddha.
If he says:
"I saw light emerge from between my eyebrows, about the size of a peck-measure; it gradually grew larger and larger, then ascended upward and leaped into the air.
He was instructed to follow the light and observe: "Which light is it that ascends?"
When his mind grew weary, he finally rested; yet he sought further on again.
He thought:
"I shall seek further until I reach the ultimate limit, arriving where light comes to its end."
These are the twenty-one matters.
Twenty-two matters were originally omitted.
According to the teaching, one should seek this Flower-Buddha starting from the East.
If one says:
"I see the light manifest; there are immeasurable subtle lights, all of which I perceive as clearly as if gazing at them.
At the ends of these lights, there are transformation Buddhas filling the eastern direction, with intervals between them of perhaps five paces."
He was instructed to continue traveling eastward to observe it.
If he says:
"I traveled and saw immeasurable Buddhas," [then it is so].
When the mind grows weary, it then ceases.
The instruction continues with the visualization reaching to the furthest distances until further signs are seen; this is likewise done for the south, west, and north.
These are the twenty-three matters.
The teaching is to observe one's own body.
If one says:
"I see my own body as entirely luminous and pure, like a mass of light."
Instruct them to visualize the Buddha, perform prostrations in sequence, and make offerings.
If they say:
"I see immeasurable Buddhas arrayed in rows; I hold various flowers and scatter them one after another as offerings, pervading all the Buddhas."
These are the twenty-four matters.
He instructs them to contemplate these flowers being offered.
If they say:
"I see that where the flowers fall near the Buddha, they immediately form flower canopies; their rows and ranks are orderly, magnificent, and exquisite, all being exactly like this."
"In this manner, all these Buddhas are seated upon their couches within the canopies.
These are the twenty-five matters for teaching the contemplation of the flower canopy.
If one says:
"I see the flower-canopy gradually rising higher, leaping into the air and merging into a single parasol that covers all Buddhas," this is the twenty-sixth matter.
Instructing one to contemplate their own body, if they say:
"I see my own body as coarse and large, like a mass of light."
He instructed them to return and observe the Buddha, performing prostrations in succession until they had circled him completely, then looking up at the canopy.

If they said, "I see within the upper floral canopy a flower pedestal facing downward, made of the seven treasures, from which a flower descends; I receive it in my hands," [he would know their minds].
He instructed them to scatter offerings in all directions to make offerings to all the Buddhas so that they would reach everywhere;
this was the twenty-seventh matter.
Having instructed them to pay homage to the Buddha and complete their requests for blessings, he instructed them to sit by the Buddha’s side with single-minded devotion.
If one says:

"While I sat for but a brief moment, I saw the earth spontaneously rise up as a terrace made of the seven treasures, wondrous in color and exquisite in fragrance; I then took it to make offerings to all Buddhas."
These are the twenty-eight matters.
He instructs him to observe his own body until it is extremely clear, and he instructs him to bring it to clarity.
He instructs him to sit beside the Buddha and observe the flowers used for the offering.
If one says:
"I see these flowers beneath the Buddha’s feet, which have transformed into a seat of lapis lazuli.
They are arranged in successive rows for the Buddha to sit upon; the pathways between them are all composed of superior jewels, straight and incomparable."
These are the twenty-nine matters.
He teaches one to observe one's own body.
If one says:
“I see within my body yet another small body appearing in two layers; looking inward, the exterior is bright and pure.
[The teacher] instructs him to again contemplate the Buddha.
If he says:
"I see all Buddhas entering into the body of a single Buddha without any crowding.
This concludes the thirty matters.
Since the deeds of the Buddha are numerous, these thirty matters have been briefly set forth to instruct the practitioner.

First, one is taught the method of the contemplation of a compassionate mind; first, one is instructed to repent, purifying body, speech, and mind, and with a sincere and earnest heart, to give rise to great vows. Only then is one taught to sit, whereupon one should contemplate one's own body with both mind and eyes.
If one says,
"I see my own body," one then contemplates the bodies of others.
If one says:

"I see sentient beings suffering before me; beneath their feet fire blazes, forming a pit of fire that burns all sinners, their bodies festering with pus and blood flowing into pools, as they cry out in loud voices at immeasurable agony."
Furthermore, one sees cities surrounding the four directions.
This is called the first matter.
It teaches one to give rise to great vows, to develop a mind of compassion, and to contemplate sentient beings with discernment.
If one says:

"I see sinners, oppressed by fire, throwing themselves into a pool of pus and blood; the pus and blood in the pool then transforms into a pit of fire that burns all the sinners, causing immeasurable suffering as they wail together without a moment's respite."
There are two matters:
instructing them to observe with clarity and not harbor fear while vowing to provide rescue; and instructing each person to take their place, even if many must do so.
If they say:
"I shall take each person in turn and place them upon the pit to allow them to recover.
These are the three matters.
He instructed them to observe this with clear discernment.
If one says:

"I see immeasurable people within the city gates who come to cast themselves into fire pits and undergo further suffering; I shall take their place to bring them out and lead them to a place of safety."
"Regarding these four matters,
instruct them to observe them closely.
If they say:
"I saw people coming through the various gates without ceasing, undergoing immeasurable suffering.
By the power of my mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), I then reached out with my own hand and touched this gate; the gate was immediately shattered, and all four walls were completely destroyed."
Regarding these five matters,
instruct them by means of the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
If they say:

"When I saw those being punished for their crimes, compassion arose within me; tears fell like rain, which I caught in my hands and scattered over the fiery pit, whereupon the fire was instantly extinguished."
"Six matters: he was instructed to observe further.

Having seen that the fire had already been extinguished and only a great pit filled with pus and blood remained, his own body emitted water which entered the pool; the bloody pool vanished and its water became clear."
"Regarding these seven matters,
instruct him to observe them closely.
If he says:"
"I see a great flowering tree growing in the pond; when sentient beings see this tree, they come to take it.
I instruct them to drink its water and bathe in it to purify their bodies."
There are eight matters.
He instructs [the disciple] to ascend the flower pedestal himself.
If he says:
"After I had ascended the flower pedestal, I saw the sentient beings below who also desired to ascend; I immediately pulled them up and placed them within the petals.
Because the flower was narrow and small, it could not accommodate them; I then rubbed it with my hand to make the flower expand so that they could fit inside."
Regarding these nine matters,
once he has been instructed to contemplate his own body as luminous and pure,
if he says:

"I also saw various sinners who were hungry and in need of food; giving rise to a heart of compassion, food and drink immediately appeared by my side, which I gave to them all so that they might be fully satisfied and find rest. All those people said that they had left suffering behind and attained happiness."
Regarding these ten matters, he instructed him to observe them closely:

"The flower pedestal grows with several tiers emerging one after another; I then ascended it to the second tier, and once my body was settled in a stable posture, I called out to those below to all ascend the flower pedestal so that they might dwell there in comfort."

I gave rise to a heart of compassion; thereupon, I provided them with food and drink until they were fully satisfied. With a mind of loving-kindness, I immediately preached the Dharma for them, saying:
"Because of various evil karmas committed in past lives—such as using poisonous fire to burn down people's homes—you now undergo this retribution."
"You should repent and eliminate your past offenses.
(Eleventh matter.
This instruction for generating wholesome thoughts further leads one to ascend the flower pedestal.
If one says:

"I have already descended to the lower realms while others have ascended; I shall provide them with whatever they need so that they lack for nothing, and I will further preach the Dharma to them regarding the retributions of the five destinies among gods and humans, causing their minds to open and be liberated."
Regarding the twelve matters,
he instructs him to search upon the flowers. If he says:
"I have already ascended upon the flowers for the sake of those below; now, desiring that they too may ascend, I shall cause them all to ascend.

Furthermore, giving rise to a heart of joy, I observe within these flowers, and there spontaneously appear gold, silver, rare treasures, clothing, food, drink, and all necessary items, which I bestow upon them all."
The various celestial musical instruments arrived spontaneously; having enjoyed pleasures according to their desires, [the Buddha] then preached the Dharma for them, saying:
"You have given rise to virtuous minds, and their retribution has followed immediately; receive and enjoy this fruit of retribution."
"Thus are the thirteen matters.
He instructs [the practitioner] to increase the mind of joy and ascend upon the flower.
If he says:"
"Once the top of the flower pedestal has been reached, those below will feel joy in their hearts, and subsequently they shall ascend until they reach the very top of the flower.
He further instructed them to contemplate the flower.
If one says:
"I see the flower-heads.
I see the flower-heads producing large, sweet fruits, complete with both fragrance and flavor."
He addressed the people, saying:
"There are fruits upon the tree that you may take and eat.
They then ate as he had said until they were fully satisfied, and all exclaimed, "How joyful!"
Regarding these fourteen matters,
he taught the contemplation within the flower.
If one says:
"I saw a seven-jeweled platform spontaneously emerge from within a flower, and inside it was a scripture titled 'Wisdom.
I immediately issued a proclamation to all people:
'Within this is a scripture that expounds the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; you should prostrate yourselves, give rise to a mind of reverence, and make offerings of flowers and incense.'"
When he wished to listen to the Dharma again, I replied,
"Burn incense and scatter flowers.
Once the offerings were completed, he again wished to listen to the Dharma.
I then replied:
"Both I and this assembly are not yet pure; how could we hear it?
The Dharma is that which brings purity to body and mind."
They immediately accepted the instruction.
I said to the people:
"Have everyone sit upright, close your eyes, and with single-minded focus, eliminate all distracted thoughts."
I was likewise; in a mere moment, my body became entirely bright and pure, and my mind was serene. I then said to him:
"I shall now expound this wondrous Dharma for you; listen and receive it with a sincere heart."
He immediately accepted the instruction.
I preached the Dharma for him, enabling him to hear the teaching.
Once he had heard the Dharma, there was a natural radiance in the sky above that illuminated this flower pedestal, causing all people in the four directions to see clearly and purely.
These people, seeing the light, were filled with joy; their bodies felt light and they leaped for joy, following the light as it departed.
(Fifteenth matter:
Teaching the contemplation of the body.)
If one says:
"I personally see light emerge from my body, circling its four sides; as this radiance becomes increasingly intense, I then use my own hand to push this light far out toward the four directions."
Countless people followed the light and arrived; with a mind of loving-kindness, I provided them with their necessities, ensuring they were fully satisfied and lacked for nothing.
I then preached the Dharma to them, causing them to attain faith, understanding, joy, and to practice it. In a mere moment, they leaped into the air and departed, circling about as they went.
"Sixteen matters.
Instructing them to contemplate the flower pedestal with true discernment. If they say:"
"I see that everything belonging to the flower-throne has already departed; I can see nothing at all, and the four directions are pure.
Within this matter, the objects of experience are also many; I have merely set forth what exists in brief.
Next, instruct them to practice the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-bhāvanā*). First, instruct them to contemplate their own bodies with a mind of loving-kindness.
Once they see [their own bodies] clearly, then instruct them to contemplate sentient beings who are suffering.
If one says:
"I see within the four mountains a great hell, filled with sinners undergoing intense suffering.
In an instant, an iron lid suddenly appears, covering the sinners so that they cannot be seen."
This was the first matter.
He instructed him to arouse a mind of loving-kindness and make a great vow:

"I shall rescue and deliver immeasurable sentient beings suffering in affliction and cause them to attain liberation. Thereupon, he gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness, sat upon the iron lid, and shattered that iron lid.
If one says:
"With this hand I shall shatter the iron lid until it is completely destroyed, and then I will look down and behold the various sinners undergoing great suffering."

There are heavy iron wheels upon their heads, or within their bodies, or beneath their feet—whether large or small—from which pus and blood flow forth; their suffering is immeasurable, and they wail aloud with cries that cannot be endured.
Furthermore, he saw immeasurable instruments for punishing criminals being used to punish those offenders, their suffering being so immeasurable that it could not be fully described.
These were the two matters.
He was further instructed to arouse vows and to observe this with an even more increased heart of compassion.
If one says:
"When I saw this sinner, compassion arose in my heart and tears fell like rain, so that all people may find a brief respite"—
these are three matters.
He taught them to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness; he would lift all the sinners to a high place so that they might find rest.
In a mere moment, everyone was thus [relieved].
These are the four matters.
He was instructed to observe it further. He said:

"I see high embankments rising on all four sides of the hells, with pools of pus and blood in their midst. Suddenly, fires break out in the four corners of these pools, burning the sinners; their suffering is unbearable as they wail and cry out in resentment."
If one says:

"Upon seeing this event, I gave rise to a heart of compassion; immediately from my own body, my hands produced clear water, which I sprinkled in the four directions to cause the fire to gradually extinguish, so that he might find some small measure of rest."
"Five matters:
instruct him to observe further.
If he says:"
"I saw immeasurable people coming from the mountains to enter the hells, undergoing various pains beyond measure.
Having seen this, compassion arose in my heart; I then erected rafts at the edge of the pond to take the place of those sinners, placing them upon the rafts so that they might find rest."
"Every person is like this.
These are the six matters;
teach them to contemplate these with clarity.
If one says:
"I see people coming and going incessantly among these mountains, suffering unceasingly.
By the power of my mind of loving-kindness, I shall grind away these mountains and turn them into level ground."
"Seven matters.
He instructs them with a mind of loving-kindness, sits in mid-air above this pond, and from his body issues a small amount of water that pours into the pond.
If one says:"
"Once I had sat in mid-air, I descended into the pool. The pus and blood in the pool flowed out in all four directions, and the pool became clear.
In a brief moment, fire broke out on all four sides of the pool, burning away this pus and blood until it was completely exhausted."
These are the eight matters.
He instructed him to sit by the pond with a mind of compassion and observe the four directions intently.
If he should say:
"I see the instruments of iron wheels and poison coming toward my seat and forming a great platform beneath it, while all the offenders each reach places of safety in the four directions."
"On the stage, I saw a fire break out; the entire stage was consumed by flames, and the fire spread in the four directions, burning everything it reached until nothing remained.
These are the nine matters.
Instruct them to observe the pond.
If they say:

"I see the spring water in the pond expanding until it reaches the four directions without limit, and within it lotus flowers grow, gradually expanding until they cover the entire surface of the pond."

While the teaching was being given amidst the flowers, he looked in the four directions and saw immeasurable people at the four sides of the pond wishing to come toward him; he instructed them to bathe so that their bodies would become pure.
Once his body was purified, he opened a small portion among the flowers and leaves; then, standing upon the lower water amidst the pathways, he caused all the people to ascend the flower pedestals.
"Ten matters:
instructing one to observe the four sides of the pond.
If one says:"
"I see that on all four sides of the pond there are pavilions that have spontaneously emerged, joined with the flowers, so that these people may ascend these pavilions and find swift rest."
Each one said to themselves, "Although we have obtained pleasure, once it has ceased, we shall immediately crave food and drink.
Having nothing with which to provide for them, he caused rain to fall from his ten fingers; the falling rain turned into milk, and all the people were made fully satisfied.
These are the eleven matters.
He instructs them to observe the interior of the flower pedestal.
If they say:
"I saw that within the flower-pedestal there emerged another pedestal, and that the towers on the four sides likewise each had an additional layer, as vast as the previous ones.
Having ascended to them, I opened a small portion among the petals and provided ladders and steps for the people to ascend."
Furthermore, atop the platform, there are towers facing the four directions; one faces east according to the direction from which one arrives, and the same applies to the other three sides.
Moreover, with a heart of compassion, one contemplates that within these flowers there are naturally provided all necessary things, sufficient to satisfy the people of the four quarters.
He then preached the Dharma for them, saying:
"This body is suffering and possesses no solidity or strength; it is entirely due to the commission of the five heinous crimes and evil deeds in past lives that one undergoes such agony."
"Now you may perform repentance.
Immediately following these words, he performed repentance.
These are the twelve matters.
Instruct them to visualize the lotus pedestal.
If they say, "Within my lotus pedestal there further emerges a multi-storied pavilion," then I shall immediately ascend it; having arrived, I shall again create a ladder and steps.

Once everyone had ascended and each had rested upon the towers, I would take from the flowers whatever food, drink, clothing, or other necessities were required, and distribute them in the four directions so that no one lacked anything.
He then preached the Dharma for them; immeasurable benefits arose, they conceived faith, and they all received and upheld the precepts of fasting, practicing them in full.
This was the thirteenth matter.
He then instructed them to further contemplate the flower pedestals and pavilions.
If one says:
"I see that the flower-pavilions and towers have arisen as before, yet they are more subtle and superior than before.

Having searched for and ascended the upper stories together with the others as previously done, I and the others each ascended the towers; together with the others, we then obtained full satisfaction so that nothing was lacking."
He further preached the Dharma for them, and they immediately accepted the teaching, all attaining benefit.
(The fourteenth matter:
He taught them to give rise to a heart of joy and contemplate intently within the flower.
If one says:
"The pavilions within my lotus pedestal have arisen as before; once I and all these people have ascended together, I shall sit upon the flower with a joyful heart."

In a brief moment, he saw that the flower-platforms and towers had all turned golden, composed of the seven precious gems. Upon them appeared inexhaustible treasuries of clothing, food, drink, fine and soft fabrics, and lutes and musical instruments; whatever one desired was obtained, and they were fully satisfied.
He further preached the Dharma for them, and they all received and practiced it.
(Fifteenth matter.
He instructed them to further observe the center of the flower pedestal.
If he says:
"I saw a tree emerge from within the flower pedestal, ten *zhang* high with flourishing branches and leaves producing fragrant and exquisite medicinal herbs.

Having climbed to the top of the tree, I looked down and saw that the lower pavilions had collapsed from the bottom up to the fifth story; the people were terrified and each cried out, 'Alas, what suffering! Then I sought the flowers and was among them."
These are the sixteen matters.
He teaches with compassion to rescue and deliver all people.
If he says:
"Within the flowers and leaves, he drew out the people and placed them upon the flower-heads; he then provided them all with sweet fruits so that they lacked for nothing.

He then preached the Dharma for them, teaching them to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to extinguish all evils, whereby their bodies and minds attained purity. They were filled with immeasurable joy and flew through the void, departing wherever they wished."
"Seventeen matters:
the instruction is to look far in the four directions from atop a flower.
If one says:"

"I saw a cloud-canopy of light coming from the four directions toward my body; at that time, light also issued from my own body and joined with the canopy, which I then stroked with my hand to cause it to expand."
Regarding these eighteen matters,
the instruction begins by following the light from the east.
If one says:

"I followed the light eastward for a very great distance; within that light, I saw immeasurable people coming from the light toward the place where the flowers were. Following them in this manner until I reached the dwelling place of the light, I then returned of my own accord to the flowers."
He instructs them in the sequential stages of practice and provides them with clothing, food, and all necessary requisites so that they may have them in abundance.

He then preaches the Dharma for them; according to their inclinations, they joyfully accept and practice it. Their bodies become light and they leap up, soaring through the air and traveling wherever they wish—south, west, and north, as well as the same.
The nineteenth matter:
He teaches the contemplation of the body so that it becomes vast, filling the void with extreme clarity and purity.

Furthermore, he clearly perceives immeasurable people from the four directions gathering around his body; through a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he causes them to enter within his body, and once they have entered his body, they abide there in peace.
In a mere moment, all things naturally required appeared; according to their wishes, these were bestowed upon all people so that none lacked anything, each attaining sufficiency, joy, and peace.
He then preached the Dharma for them, providing immeasurable benefit and causing them to attain understanding; they then departed as they pleased.
These are twenty matters.
Such instances are extremely numerous; I have merely mentioned these few matters regarding those who received the Dharma in brief.
There are three grades of physical ailments; among these, diseases caused by wind, cold, and heat are minor.

There are three types of mental afflictions that plague the body, causing one to undergo various sufferings for kalpas whenever they arise. Only the Buddha, the skilled physician, bestows the medicine of the Dharma; those who can receive and practice it eliminate the disease of birth and death.

It causes the mind to become resolute and focused without distraction, just as a person who sees a thief remains calm and composed, firmly armoring themselves so that the thief naturally retreats and disperses;
the evil thieves of a distracted mind are likewise thus.
Thus it is said:
"Though flesh and blood may be exhausted, the skin, sinews, and bones remain.

One does not abandon diligence; like a person whose body is on fire who seeks only to extinguish the flames and has no other recourse, so too is the emergence from the suffering of afflictions. One should endure the hardships of these five matters:
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, resentment, and so forth.
One should avoid clamor and bustle, delighting instead in quietude. Why is this?
The clamor of the multitude disrupts meditative concentration as if entering a forest of thorns.
Regarding the method of the four immeasurable contemplations:
those who seek the path of the Buddha should practice the four immeasurable minds.
Because his mind is immeasurable, his merit is likewise immeasurable.
Among all sentient beings, there are generally three categories:
first, those such as parents, relatives, and virtuous friends; second, enemies and malicious persons who constantly seek to harm and afflict; and third, neutral persons who are neither kin nor foes.

Regarding these three classes of people, the practitioner should regard them with a mind of loving-kindness as if they were their own kin: the elderly as fathers and the young as sons; one should always cultivate such a mind of loving-kindness.
People harbor resentment because of adverse conditions; yet when those adverse conditions are exhausted, they turn into kinship. Thus, kinship and resentment are not fixed. Why is this?
Those who are enemies in this life may become kin in a future life.

The evil of anger causes one to lose great benefit; one who loses the mind of loving-kindness creates obstacles to the Buddha-way. Therefore, one should regard those who are hateful, resentful, and hostile as if they were one's own kinsmen.
Why is this so? It is because these enemies and bandits have enabled me to attain Buddhahood.
If these enemies had not harbored ill will toward me, from what would patience have arisen?
These are my true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), who enable me to attain the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

Having attained a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*) toward enemies and thieves, I extend a mind of loving-kindness and affection toward all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, universally encompassing them all; and toward even the most minute insects and crawling creatures who find no peace, I give rise to a mind of compassion (*karuṇācitta*).
If one sees sentient beings obtain happiness in the present life, the happiness of rebirth in heaven, or the happiness of the noble path, one gives rise to a mind of joy.

Not perceiving sentient beings as having matters of suffering or happiness, one is neither attached nor delighted; governing oneself through wisdom, one gives rise to a mind of equanimity while taking sentient beings as the object of focus.
These are called the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Because loving-kindness (*maitrī*) pervades all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, they are termed "immeasurable.
A practitioner should cultivate these minds; should a mind of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) arise at any time—like a snake or fire upon one's body—it should be immediately eliminated.
If the mind wanders and scatters into the five desires, or is shrouded by the five hindrances, one should employ the power of wisdom and diligence to restrain it and bring it back.

Cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, constantly mindful of sentient beings so that they may attain the bliss of Buddhahood; practicing this without ceasing, one will then be able to leave the five desires behind and eliminate the five hindrances.

Regarding the characteristics of entering the first dhyāna: joy and bliss pervade the entire body; one gives rise to rapturous joy within all wholesome dharmas and perceives various subtle and wondrous forms; this is called the initial gateway for entering the Buddha-way.

Having attained the four immeasurable minds through the causes and conditions of meditative concentration and merit, one practices patience and remains free from anger toward all sentient beings; this is called patience toward sentient beings.
Once one has attained the patience toward sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*), it is easy to attain the patience toward dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).
This patience toward dharmas refers to the ultimate mark of emptiness wherein all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished.

One who is able to believe in and accept this patience toward dharmas is said to have attained the patience toward non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) and receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Those who wish to attain the Buddha-way should practice in this manner.

Seeking the first dhyāna, one first practices such contemplations as the contemplation of impurity, the contemplation of causes and conditions, the Buddha-recollection samādhi, or ānāpāna; thereafter, one attains entry into the various meditative concentrations.
For one who seeks the Buddha-way, it is easy to enter the first dhyāna if they first practice the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).

If a person of sharp faculties seeks the first dhyāna directly, they contemplate the various faults and afflictions of the five desires as being like a pit of fire or a latrine, and they contemplate the stage of the first dhyāna as being like a cool pond or a pavilion; thus the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are eliminated, and they immediately attain the first dhyāna.

For example, when the seer Udraka Rāmaputra first practiced dhyāna, he saw a corpse on the road that was bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling; as he contemplated it with focused attention, he saw his own body as no different from it, and through single-minded mindfulness in a quiet place, he attained the first dhyāna.
While the Buddha was sitting in meditation by the banks of the Ganges River, a monk of little learning asked him,
"How does one attain the Way?
The Buddha replied:
"Do not take other things.
He then understood the emptiness of dharmas and immediately attained the stage of the Path.
A man of great learning, marveling that he himself had gained nothing, questioned the Buddha about it.
The Buddha said,
"Take a small stone from the Ganges River and wash it thoroughly with water from a *kumbha*.
The bhikṣu did as instructed.
The Buddha asked, "Which is more:
the water of the Ganges River or the water in this ritual pitcher?
He replied:
"The Ganges cannot serve as a comparison.
The Buddha said,
"If one does not wash with one's fingers, though the water be abundant, it is of no benefit."
"The practitioner should apply diligent effort, using the fingers of wisdom and concentration to wash away the defilements of the mind.
If one does not do so, one cannot escape suffering.

Regarding the method of the contemplation of impurity: greed, hatred, and delusion are the roots of all maladies. Attachment to the body and clinging to desire give rise to hatred; being deluded by inversions is precisely because one is shrouded by ignorance.

Regarding the internal and external body, one harbors an attachment to the perception of purity; having practiced this for a long time, it is deeply ingrained and difficult to dispel. If one wishes to abandon desire, one should contemplate impurity.
Hatred arises from external objects; nevertheless, it can still be restrained.
It is like a person splitting bamboo: the first node is the most difficult to split.
Once greed and desire are subdued, the other two [afflictions] will naturally cease.

Regarding the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one should contemplate this body: it was born in an impure place within the womb; it emerged from impurity and is covered by a thin skin, yet its interior is entirely impure, being filled by the four great elements transformed into food and drink.

One observes for oneself from head to foot that within this thin skin there is not a single pure thing; there is brain membrane, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, excrement, urine, and so forth—briefly stated, there are thirty-six such substances, but in detail, they are immeasurable.
It is just as a farmer opens his granary and skillfully distinguishes between hemp, wheat, millet, and beans.

The practitioner deeply contemplates this body as a granary, seeing its various impurities and thirty-six constituent substances; by discerning the internal body as it truly is, one should know that the external body is no different from this.
If the mind abides in its proper state, the body becomes supple and the spirit experiences joy.
If the mind does not abide, one should reproach it, saying:
"For countless kalpas, I have followed you, thereby traversing the three miserable realms and undergoing endless suffering."
"From this day forward, I shall serve and attend to you; you should follow me.
Thus he withdraws his mind and brings it to accomplishment.
If his body becomes exhausted, he should contemplate white bones; by this means, he may also enter the first dhyāna.
If a practitioner aspires to the Mahāyāna, at the end of their life they will be reborn before any of the Buddhas according to their wishes.
If this does not occur, they will certainly be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven and behold Maitreya; of this there is no doubt.
The defects of the first dhyāna are that internally there are applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra), and externally there is the disaster of fire.
The defects of the second dhyāna are that internally there is joy and bliss (prīti-sukha), and externally there is the disaster of water.
The defects of the third dhyāna are that internally there is breathing and externally there is the calamity of wind.
Within the stage of the fourth dhyāna, all defects are exhausted, and it is not reached by the three calamities.
The twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) are as follows:
The four continents, the six heavens of the desire realm, the four evil destinies, the four dhyāna stages, the Great Brahmā Heaven, and the formless realm.
Within the fourth dhyāna stage there are five classes of Anāgāmin heavens; together these constitute the twenty-five states of existence.
